title: Home regulator outside IOSCO
facts: Halden Value Fund, a regulated fund
Not an IOSCO MMoU (Appendix A) signatory, and no bilateral MoU with SEBI
Its home country, not an IFSC
opts: Yes, as Category II
No. It fails the home-regulator test in Reg 4(d)
Yes, if its manager is from a FATF member country
Yes, as Category I, because it is regulated
why: Reg 4(d) requires the applicant to be resident in a country whose securities regulator has signed the IOSCO MMoU (Appendix A) or has a bilateral MoU with SEBI. The two exceptions are a government investor from a country approved by the Government of India, and an applicant set up in an IFSC.
no: Choosing a category doesn't cure eligibility. Reg 4 applies to every category, so Category II is still blocked.
The FATF-manager test only helps an applicant get into Category I under Reg 5. It doesn't override Reg 4(d).
Being regulated affects the category, but the applicant has to pass Reg 4(d) first.
cite: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(d) and proviso; Op. Guidelines Part A 2(i)
q1s: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 4(d)
q1: (d) the applicant is a resident of the country whose securities market regulator is a signatory to the International Organization of Securities Commission's Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (Appendix A Signatories) or a signatory to the bilateral Memorandum of Understanding with the Board: Provided that an applicant being Government or Government related investor shall be considered as eligible for registration, if such applicant is a resident in the country as may be approved by the Government of India;

title: Bank whose central bank isn't in the BIS
facts: Commercial bank, licensed by its home banking regulator
Not a member of the Bank for International Settlements
Category I, as a regulated bank
opts: Category I, as a bank regulated by its home banking regulator
Category II, which the guidelines allow for such banks
Not eligible in any category, because of the BIS test
Category I, once RBI approves the application
why: A bank applicant is expected to come from a country whose central bank is a BIS member (Reg 4(e)). The guidelines let a bank regulated at home whose central bank isn't a BIS member seek registration under Category II instead.
no: Category I for a bank assumes its central bank is a BIS member, which isn't the case here.
Too strict. The guidelines expressly let this bank apply under Category II.
No RBI approval converts this into Category I. RBI is consulted only for banks with an Indian presence.
cite: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(e); Op. Guidelines Part A 3(i)
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 3(i)
q1: In case a bank FPI applicant is regulated by the banking sector regulator in its home jurisdiction, but the central bank of that country is not a member of BIS, the FPI can seek registration under Category II.

title: Foreign bank with an Indian branch
facts: Proprietary investment arm of a European bank
The bank has a branch in Mumbai
q: What extra step applies before you register it?
opts: None. Process it like any other Category I bank
Send it to SEBI first, which gets RBI's comments
Ask the applicant to get RBI's approval directly
Register it now, then tell RBI within 7 working days of approval
why: When the applicant or its group entity is a bank with a branch or representative office in India, or is a central bank, the DDP sends the form to SEBI. SEBI asks RBI for comments and passes them to the DDP to consider. This isn't repeated at continuance.
no: The Indian branch triggers a reference to SEBI and RBI. Skipping it is a process breach.
The DDP routes the form through SEBI. The applicant doesn't go to RBI itself.
RBI's comments come before registration, not after it.
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 3(i)
q1: In case an applicant/ its group entity is (i) bank or its subsidiary and has a bank branch/representative office in India or (ii) a central bank or its subsidiary, the respective DDP shall forward the application form to SEBI. SEBI would in turn request RBI to provide its comments. Based on the comments received from RBI, SEBI would notify the comments of RBI to DDP to consider while processing such applications.

title: Unregulated Luxembourg partnership
facts: Luxembourg AIFM, appropriately regulated, registered with SEBI as a Category I FPI
Manager accepts responsibility for the fund's acts and omissions
opts: Category I
Category II, because the fund itself is unregulated
Not eligible
Category II until the fund is regulated
why: Under Reg 5(a)(iv)(II), an unregulated fund from a FATF member country is Category I when its manager is appropriately regulated, is registered as a Category I FPI, and takes responsibility for the fund's acts and omissions. Luxembourg is a FATF member.
no: Reg 5(a)(iv)(II) lets an unregulated fund from a FATF country take Category I through a regulated Category I manager.
Unregulated funds can register. Reg 5(b)(viii) even lists them under Category II.
Category I is available now, without the fund being regulated.
q1s: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 5(a)(iv)
q1: (iv) Entities from the Financial Action Task Force member countries , or from any country specified by the Central Government by an order or by way of an agreement or treaty with other sovereign Governments, which are – I. appropriately regulated funds; II. unregulated funds whose investment manager is appropriately regulated and registered as a Category I foreign portfolio investor: Provided that the investment manager undertakes the responsibility of all the acts of commission or omission of such unregulated fund;

title: Cayman fund, New York manager
facts: Halcyon Opportunities Fund Ltd, Cayman Islands
New York adviser, registered with SEBI as a Category I FPI
Manager accepts responsibility for the fund
opts: Category II, because Cayman isn't a FATF member
Category I, under Reg 5(a)(v)(A)
Not eligible
Category I only if Cayman regulates the fund
why: Reg 5(a)(v)(A) looks at the manager, not where the fund sits. An entity whose manager is from a FATF member country and is registered as a Category I FPI qualifies for Category I, provided the manager takes responsibility. Without that registration and undertaking, the fund would fall to Category II.
no: That would be right under Reg 5(a)(iv), which looks at the fund's country. Reg 5(a)(v)(A) looks at the manager's.
Nothing here fails the Reg 4 eligibility tests, and unregulated funds can register.
The fund doesn't need to be regulated. The manager route gives Category I.
q1s: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 5(a)(v)
q1: (v) An entity (A) whose investment manager is from the Financial Action Task Force member country and such an investment manager is registered as a Category I foreign portfolio investor; or (B) which is at least seventy-five per cent owned, directly or indirectly by another entity, eligible under sub-clause (ii), (iii) and (iv) of clause (a) of this regulation and such an eligible entity is from a Financial Action Task Force member country: Provided that such an investment manager or eligible entity undertakes the responsibility of all the acts of commission or omission of the applicants seeking registration under this sub-clause.

title: NRI general partner runs the fund
facts: An NRI is the general partner. The manager isn't registered with SEBI.
opts: Yes. Both percentages are inside the limits
No. NRIs can't be in control of the applicant
Yes, but only if it registers as a Category II FPI instead
No. Total NRI money has to stay under 25%
why: Three tests apply: each NRI, OCI or RI below 25%, all of them together below 50%, and none of them in control. The control test has carve-outs: an offshore fund with a SEBI NOC under the Mutual Fund Regulations, or a manager controlled by NRIs that is regulated at home and registered with SEBI as a non-investing FPI, or set up and registered in India. None applies here.
no: The percentages pass, but the control test fails. All three tests have to be met.
The control test is an eligibility condition, so changing the category doesn't fix it.
25% is the cap for a single NRI, OCI or RI. The cap on all of them together is below 50%.
cite: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 4(c); Op. Guidelines Part A 2(ii)(a)–(d)
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 2(ii)
q1: Where NRIs or OCI or RIs are constituents of the applicant – a. the contribution of a single NRI or OCI or RI shall be below twenty-five percent of the total contribution in the corpus of the applicant; b. the aggregate contribution of NRIs, OCIs and RIs shall be below fifty percent of the total contribution in the corpus of the applicant. Explanation: The contribution of RI is permitted, if made through the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) approved by Reserve Bank of India in global funds whose Indian exposure is less than 50%. c. the NRIs, OCIs and RIs shall not be in control of the applicant.

title: Redemptions push NRI share over 50%
facts: Other investors redeem; NRI/OCI share rises to 53%
opts: Sell all Indian holdings within 5 trading days of the breach
90 days to fix it, then a purchase block and a 180-day exit
No action needed, because a passive breach doesn't count
Stop all trading today and report the breach to SEBI
why: A temporary breach of the NRI/OCI/RI limits gives the FPI 90 days to comply again. If it is still in breach after 90 days, it can't make fresh purchases and must sell its positions within the following 180 days.
no: 5 trading days is the timeline for breaching an investment limit, not for breaching the investor-mix limits.
A temporary breach still counts. The 90-day period exists to fix exactly this.
Nothing is blocked on day one. The FPI gets 90 days to comply first.
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 2(ii)(f)
q1: In case of temporary breach of above investment limits after December 31. 2020, the foreign portfolio investor shall comply with the eligibility conditions within ninety days of its breach. In case the foreign portfolio investor remains non-compliant with the said requirement even after ninety days, then no fresh purchases shall be permitted and such foreign portfolio investor shall liquidate its existing position in Indian securities market within a period of the next one hundred and eighty days.

title: Two sister FPIs cross 10% together
opts: Fine. Each FPI is below 10% on its own, so no breach
Breach. Sell the excess in 5 trading days or it all becomes FDI
Fine, as long as the aggregate FPI limit still has room
Breach, and the exchange reverses B's new purchase to cure it
why: Common ownership above 50%, or common control, puts FPIs in one investor group, and their holdings count together against the below-10% limit on a fully diluted basis. If the excess isn't sold within 5 trading days of settlement, the group's entire investment in the company is treated as FDI, and it can't make further portfolio investment in that company.
no: Common ownership above 50% makes them one investor group, so the limit applies to the combined 10.3%.
The aggregate FPI limit is a separate cap at company level. The 10% group limit still applies.
Exchange trades aren't reversed. The fix is to sell down within 5 trading days, or the holding turns into FDI.
q1s: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, Regulation 20(7)
q1: (7) The purchase of equity shares of each company by a single foreign portfolio investor including its investor group shall be below ten per cent of the total paid-up equity capital on a fully diluted basis of the company: Provided that where the total investment under these regulations by a foreign portfolio investor including its investor group exceeds the threshold of below ten per cent of the total paid up equity capital in a listed or to be listed company on a fully diluted basis, the foreign portfolio investor shall divest the excess holding within five trading days from the date of settlement of the trades resulting in the breach: Provided further that in case the foreign portfolio investor fails to divest the excess holding, the entire investment in the company by such foreign portfolio investor including its investor group shall be considered as investment under the Foreign Direct Investment, as per the procedure specified by the Board and the foreign portfolio investor and its investor group shall not make further portfolio investment in that company under these regulations,

title: Two UCITS under one management company
facts: Luxembourg UCITS, holds 6% of Company Y
Irish UCITS, holds 5% of Company Y
Same management company (common control); no common ownership above 50%
q: Are they combined for the 10% limit?
opts: Yes. Common control makes them one investor group
No. That rule doesn't apply to regulated public retail funds
Yes, unless SEBI grants these two funds a specific exemption order
No, because they are domiciled in different countries
why: Reg 22(4) switches off the common-control rule where the FPIs are appropriately regulated public retail funds, or retail funds with regulated managers. The relief covers common control only. If they also shared more than 50% ownership, they would still be combined.
no: Normally yes, but Reg 22(4) switches off the common-control rule for appropriately regulated public retail funds.
The exemption is written into Reg 22(4) itself. No SEBI order is needed.
Country doesn't decide investor groups. Ownership and control do.

q1: (4) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-regulation (3), the clubbing of investment limit of foreign portfolio investors having common control shall not be applicable where – (a) foreign portfolio investors are appropriately regulated public retail funds; or (b) the foreign portfolio investors are public retail funds where the majority is owned by appropriately regulated public retail fund on look through basis; or (c) foreign portfolio investors are public retail funds and investment managers of such foreign portfolio investors are appropriately regulated. Explanation - Public retail funds means (i) mutual funds or unit trusts which are open for subscription to retail investors and which do not have specific investor type requirements like accredited investors; (ii) insurance companies where segregated portfolio with one to one correlation with a single investor is not maintained; and (iii)pension funds.

title: Ownership change reported eight months late
facts: Category I fund managed by an asset manager
New parent bought 70% of the asset manager on 10 January 2026
opts: Update the records. Late reporting has no consequence
Re-assess eligibility and report the delay to SEBI
Cancel the registration for the late intimation
Block the account permanently for the breach
why: Any direct or indirect change in structure, ownership or control must be reported within 7 working days. The DDP has to re-assess eligibility. Where the FPI was more than six months late, the DDP must report the case to SEBI with the reason.
no: A delay over six months has to go to SEBI, and the change itself needs an eligibility check.
DDPs don't cancel registrations. That is SEBI's decision under the Intermediaries Regulations.
There's no automatic permanent block. The DDP re-assesses eligibility and escalates the delay.
cite: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 22(1)(c), Reg 31(2)(e); Op. Guidelines Part A 15
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 15
q1: In terms of Regulation 22(1)(c), if there is any change in the material information previously furnished by the FPI to the DDP and/or SEBI, which has a bearing on the certificate granted by the DDP on behalf of the Board or relating to any direct or indirect change in its structure or ownership or control, change in regulatory status, merger, demerger or restructuring, change in category/ sub-category / structure/ jurisdiction/ name of FPI/ beneficial ownership etc, of the FPI, it shall forthwith inform the DDP and/or the Board in writing. The DDP shall examine all such material changes and re-assess the eligibility of the FPI including requiring FPIs to seek fresh registration. However, DDP shall not process any request for change in jurisdiction of the FPI and in such cases, FPI may apply for new FPI registration. Where there is a delay of more than six months in intimation of material change by the FPI to the DDP, the DDP shall, forthwith, inform all such cases to SEBI for appropriate action, if any, along with reason for delay.

title: Fund moves from Dublin to Luxembourg
facts: Change the country on the existing registration
q: Can the DDP make the change?
opts: Yes. Update the registration and its country code
No. It needs a new FPI registration
Yes, but only with SEBI's prior written approval
Yes, because both countries are FATF members
why: The DDP re-assesses most material changes, but it can't process a change in the FPI's jurisdiction. The FPI has to apply for a new registration.
no: The guidelines specifically bar DDPs from processing a change of jurisdiction.
There's no SEBI approval route for this. A fresh registration is the only option.
FATF membership is irrelevant here. A change of jurisdiction can't be processed on an existing registration at all.
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 15(ii)
q1: The DDP shall examine all such material changes and re-assess the eligibility of the FPI including requiring FPIs to seek fresh registration. However, DDP shall not process any request for change in jurisdiction of the FPI and in such cases, FPI may apply for new FPI registration.

title: Renewal fee paid seven weeks late
facts: Take the fee now and continue the registration
q: What do you tell the client?
opts: Fine. Accept the fee with a written reason for the delay
Not possible. Surrender, then file a fresh application
Allowed, since it's still within 90 days of expiry
Allowed, but only with SEBI's specific permission
why: A registration stops being valid after the date fees were paid up to, and continuance can't be applied for after expiry. The entity must surrender and apply fresh. Fees and updates should reach the DDP at least 15 days before validity ends.
no: A reason for delay covers renewal papers that arrive late but before expiry. After expiry, continuance isn't possible.
There's no 90-day grace period after expiry.
The guidelines give no SEBI permission route. It has to surrender and reapply.
cite: Op. Guidelines Part A 5(iii)–(vi); FPI Regs 2019, Reg 9(3)
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 5
q1: Where the FPI has not paid fees for continuance of its registration, its FPI registration shall cease to be valid after the date, up to which, the last registration fees were duly paid by the FPI. An FPI cannot apply for continuance after expiry of its registration. However, if such entity intends to have FPI registration, it will have to make a fresh application for registration after surrender of its earlier FPI registration.

title: Broker investing for its clients
facts: Category II, to invest client money
Two individuals, one family office, one trading company
q: Can all four clients invest through this registration?
opts: Yes. All four would be eligible as FPIs on their own
No. The trading company can't be a client
Yes, if the broker also holds a Category I registration
No. Brokers can't invest on behalf of clients at all
why: Regulated entities can invest for clients as Category II FPIs, but those clients must be individuals or family offices, must themselves be eligible as FPIs, and can't act for third parties. Client details go to the DDP every quarter.
no: Being FPI-eligible is necessary but not enough. The client also has to be an individual or a family office.
A Category I registration covers the broker's own money. It doesn't widen who the client registration can serve.
Regulated entities, brokers included, can invest for clients through a Category II registration.
cite: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 5(b)(vii); Op. Guidelines Part A 3(iv)
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 3(iv)
q1: Where such entities are undertaking investments on behalf of their clients, Category II FPI registration shall be granted subject to following conditions: Clients of FPI can only be individuals and family offices.

title: Major investor added to UN sanctions list
facts: An investor holding 30% of the corpus is added to the UN Security Council Sanctions List
A sell order on Indian holdings
opts: Block new buys but let the pending sell go through
Block all buying and selling, and notify SEBI
Allow trading normally until SEBI writes in
Freeze only that investor's share of the fund
why: If the FPI or a material underlying investor comes under UNSC sanctions, the custodian must stop all further buying and selling in the account and notify SEBI immediately.
no: Allowing sales is the rule when a home country loses compliant status. Sanctions block selling too.
The custodian acts first and then notifies SEBI. It doesn't wait to hear back.
The block covers the whole FPI account, not one investor's share.

q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 16(i)
q1: Further, in case the FPI itself or its underlying investors contributing twenty-five percent or more in the corpus of the FPI or identified on the basis of control, come under the Sanctions List notified by the United Nations Security Council, custodian shall not allow any further buy/sell in the account of such FPI and shall forthwith notify such instances to SEBI.

title: Home country put on the FATF high-risk list
facts: Home country listed in FATF's public statement as high-risk
opts: It must sell everything within 180 days
No fresh purchases; it may hold or sell
The registration is cancelled by the DDP
Nothing changes until the next renewal
why: When a jurisdiction stops being compliant (it leaves IOSCO, a SEBI MoU or the BIS, or FATF names it high-risk), the custodian blocks fresh purchases. The FPI may keep or sell what it holds, and the DDP reports the affected FPIs to SEBI.
no: There's no forced sale. The FPI can keep or sell its holdings.
The registration isn't cancelled. Fresh purchases are blocked until the jurisdiction is compliant again.
The custodian acts as soon as the status changes, not at renewal.
q1s: SEBI Operational Guidelines for FPIs and DDPs, Part A 16(i)
q1: If a jurisdiction, which was a compliant jurisdiction at the time of grant of registration to FPI, becomes non-compliant jurisdiction i.e. ceases to be member of IOSCO/ Bilateral Memorandum of Understanding with SEBI/ BIS or the concerned jurisdiction of FPI is listed in FATF public statement as "high risk" and "noncooperative" jurisdiction or the concerned jurisdiction of FPI then concerned Custodian shall not allow such FPIs to make fresh purchases till the time the jurisdiction/FPI is compliant with the Regulations. However, the FPI shall be allowed to sell the securities or continue to hold the securities already purchased by it. The concerned DDP shall inform to SEBI details of such FPIs upon such change.

title: Rejected for missing papers
facts: DDP A, for incomplete documents and unpaid fee
opts: Ask SEBI to reconsider within 30 days
Fix the gaps and reapply, with any DDP
Wait six months before reapplying anywhere
Reapply only through DDP A, which rejected it
why: An applicant can ask SEBI to reconsider within 30 days, but not when the rejection was technical: missing information or documents, or unpaid fees. Another DDP can take the application once it has checked why it was rejected and confirmed the gaps are fixed.
no: The 30-day reconsideration route exists, but Reg 8(3) excludes technical rejections like missing documents or fees.
There's no waiting period. It can reapply as soon as the gaps are fixed.
Any DDP can take it, after checking the rejection reason in the depositories' shared database.
cite: FPI Regs 2019, Reg 8(3); Op. Guidelines Part A 7

q1: (3) The applicant, who is aggrieved by the decision of the designated depository participant under sub-regulation (1) may, within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of communication under sub-regulation (2), apply to the Board for reconsideration of the decision of the designated depository participant: Provided that such application for reconsideration shall not be considered by the Board where the rejection was on account of technical reasons such as non-submission of complete information, documents, including non-payment of specified fees.

title: 30% of a Category III AIF

opts: Yes. Category III AIF units are permitted for FPIs
No. An FPI can't hold more than 25% in a Category III AIF
Only with RBI's prior approval for the stake above 25%
Only Category II FPIs can invest in AIFs
why: FPIs can invest in units of Category III AIFs, REITs and InvITs, but a single FPI can't hold more than 25% of a Category III AIF.
no: They are permitted, but capped at 25% of any one AIF.
No RBI approval lifts the 25% cap.
Both categories can invest in Category III AIF units.

q1: A FPI shall not hold more than twenty five percent stake in a category III AIF.

title: Category II fund wants to issue P-notes
facts: Issue offshore derivative instruments on Indian equity
Mix of institutions and wealthy individuals
opts: Yes, as long as it reports them to SEBI monthly
No. Only Category I FPIs can issue ODIs
Yes, through a separate ODI-suffixed registration
Yes, but only to institutional subscribers
why: Only Category I FPIs can issue ODIs, only to persons eligible for Category I registration, and only after KYC on the subscribers.
no: Monthly reporting is a duty of eligible issuers. It doesn't make a Category II FPI eligible.
A separate registration with an "ODI" suffix keeps a Category I issuer's derivatives apart. It doesn't let a Category II FPI issue.
The issuer must be Category I, whoever the subscribers are.

q1: (a) such offshore derivative instruments are issued only by persons registered as Category I foreign portfolio investor; (b) such offshore derivative instruments are issued only to persons eligible for registration as Category I foreign portfolio investors;

title: Surrender with stranded delisted shares
facts: Delisted shares it can't sell on exchange
opts: Nothing. Residual shares don't block a surrender
Get holdings to nil, by off-market sale or write-off
Transfer the stranded shares to the custodian
Wait for SEBI to cancel the registration on its own initiative
why: The DDP asks SEBI for a no-objection certificate only after confirming nil securities, nil bank balance and nil open derivatives. Delisted shares can be sold off-market under FEMA pricing. If that fails, an FPI that intends to surrender can write them off, reported as a sale with nil proceeds.

The custodian doesn't take the shares. A write-off removes them from its books and freezes the demat account.
Surrender is a request through the DDP with SEBI's no-objection certificate. Nothing happens automatically.

q: Can this go through the FPI route?
opts: Yes, because it's well under the 10% limit
No. Buying unlisted equity is FDI
Yes, but only with SEBI's prior approval
Yes, if it's booked as an off-market transfer

no: The 10% limit only matters for securities an FPI is allowed to buy, and unlisted equity isn't one of them.
No SEBI approval brings unlisted equity into the FPI route.

title: Insurer with unit-linked sleeves

Insurance supervisor in a permitted jurisdiction
opts: Yes. Regulated insurers always qualify
No. The segregated portfolios rule it out
